findings.note: `hangata` preserves usually; the pest-pressure term stays English. Candidate says pressure usually increases for a reason without adding a cause or treatment.
All three possible contexts remain exact: stressed plants, one crop dominating the ground, or broad chemical use having already removed helpful predators.

`pele` preserves before treating anything; `sheba system yohle` preserves the instruction to look at the whole system. The broad treat verb remains a modest uncertainty, but the source ordering and scope remain explicit.
The existing localized questions retain water shortage, compacted or nutrient-hungry soil, and whether predators are already helping. Not changed by this packet.

The existing paragraph retains that a yellow leaf is not by itself proof of insects, lists water/nutrition/root damage as alternatives, and says identify which before acting. Not changed by this packet.
`mehato e mene, ka tatellano` retains four steps and their order.
The existing first step retains observing the damage pattern, leaf underside, stem and nearby plants.
The existing second step retains checking soil moisture, roots, spacing, nutrition and drainage as stress factors.

The candidate labels this as step three and says protect what is helping. The beneficial-insect claim remains exact English, preserving its helpful role and comparison to work the grower would otherwise do.

Repaired candidate keeps fourth-step and only-then sequencing in Sesotho, holds `and start with the lightest thing that works` exactly in English, and retains conditional may-help, suitability and monitoring statements verbatim.

The complete hold preserves only-if-needed treatment, product registration for both crop and pest, label compliance, neem inclusion, protection and harvest-waiting instructions, and both prohibitions against improvised mixtures and stronger doses.
The self-reflection instruction and ‘usually’ frequency are preserved; candidate asks the learner to tell themself the truth about which step they usually skip.
